stem:
Deduce the oxidation number of S in the following species:

i. \(\mathrm{SO_2}\)

ii. \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\)
solution:
i. \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) is a neutral molecule :

\(\therefore\) Sum of oxidation number of all atom of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) = 0 = (oxidation number of S) + 2 \(\times\) (oxidation number of O)

\(\therefore\) 0 = (oxidation number of S) + 2 \(\times\) (\(-2\))

\(\therefore\) Oxidation number of S in \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) = \(0 - (2 \times (-2)) = 0 - (-4) = +4\)

ii. \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) is an ionic species.

\(\therefore\) Sum of oxidation number of all atom of \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) = \(-2\) = Oxidation number of S + 4 \(\times\) (Oxidation number of O)

\(\therefore\) Oxidation number of S in \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) = \(-2 - 4 \times (-2) = -2 + 8 = +6\)
_note: p-02 right column, printed p.83. Carries its own `Solution:` label.

stem:
Assign oxidation number to each element in the following compounds or ions.

a. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\)

b. \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\)

c. \(\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}\)
solution:
**a. \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\)**

1. Oxidation number of K = \(+1\)

2. Oxidation number of O = \(-2\)

3. Sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms = 0

\(\therefore\) Oxidation no. of K + oxidation of Mn + 4 \(\times\) oxidation number of O = 0

\((+1)\) + oxidation number of Mn + \(4 \times (-2) = 0\)

oxidation number of Mn \(+ 1 - 8 = 0\)

oxidation number of Mn \(- 7 = 0\)

oxidation number of Mn = \(+7\)

**b. \(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\)**

1. oxidation number of K = \(+1\)

2. oxidation number of O = \(-2\)

3. sum of oxidation number of all atoms = 0

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation no. of K + 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of Cr + 7 \(\times\) oxidation number of O = 0

\(\therefore\) \(2 \times (+1)\) + 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of Cr + \(7 \times (-2) = 0\)

\(\therefore\) \(+2\) + 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of Cr \(- 14 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of Cr \(+ 2 - 14 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of Cr \(- 12 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of Cr = \(+12\)

\(\therefore\) oxidation number of Cr = \(+12/2\)

\(\therefore\) oxidation number of Cr = \(+6\)

**c. \(\mathrm{Ca_3(PO_4)_2}\)**

1. oxidation number of Ca = \(+2\) (alkaline earth metal ion)

2. oxidation number of O = \(-2\)

3. sum of oxidation number of all atoms = 0

\(\therefore\) 3 \(\times\) O.N. of Ca + 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of P + 8 \(\times\) oxidation number of O = 0

\(\therefore\) \(3 \times (+2)\) + 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of P \(+ 8 \times (-2) = 0\)

\(\therefore\) \((+6)\) + 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of P \(- 16 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of P \(- 16 + 6 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of P \(- 10 = 0\)

\(\therefore\) 2 \(\times\) oxidation number of P = \(+10\)

\(\therefore\) oxidation number of P = \(+10/2\)

\(\therefore\) oxidation number of P = \(+5\)
_note: Stem + start of solution in p-03 left column (printed p.84); the solution continues into the p-03 right column. Transcribed whole across the column break.

stem:
Assign oxidation number to the atoms other than O and H in the following species.

i. \(\mathrm{SO_3^{2\ominus}}\)

ii. \(\mathrm{BrO_3^{\ominus}}\)

iii. \(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}}\)

iv. \(\mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}}\)

v. \(\mathrm{NO_3^{\ominus}}\)

vi. \(\mathrm{NO_2^{\ominus}}\)

vii. \(\mathrm{SO_3}\)

viii. \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\)
solution:
The oxidation number of O atom bonded to a more electropositive atom is \(-2\) and that of H atom bonded to electronegative atom is \(+1\). Using these values the oxidation numbers of atoms of the other elements in a given polyatomic species are calculated.

i. \(\mathrm{SO_3^{2\ominus}}\)

\(-2\) = oxidation number of S + 3 \(\times\) (oxidation number of O)

\(\therefore\) Oxidation number of S = \(-2 - 3(-2) = -2 + 6 = 4\)

ii. \(\mathrm{BrO_3^{\ominus}}\)

\(-1\) = oxidation number of Br + 3 \(\times\) (oxidation number of O)

\(\therefore\) Oxidation number of Br = \(-1 - 3(-2) = -1 + 6 = 5\)

Similarly the oxidation number in the remaining species are found to be

iii. Cl in \(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}}\) : \(+7\)

iv. N in \(\mathrm{NH_4^{\oplus}}\) : \(-3\)

v. N in \(\mathrm{NO_3^{\ominus}}\) : \(+5\)

vi. N in \(\mathrm{NO_2^{\ominus}}\) : \(+3\)

vii. S in \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) : \(+6\)

viii. N in \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) : \(+5\)
_note: Stem + the opening paragraph of the solution are in the p-03 right column (printed p.84); the worked parts i–viii are at the head of p-04 (printed p.85). SPANS THE PAGE BREAK — transcribed whole.

stem:
Identify whether the following reactions are redox or not. State oxidants and reductants therein.

a. \(\mathrm{3H_3AsO_3(aq) + BrO_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow Br^{\ominus}(aq) + 3H_3AsO_4(aq)}\)
solution:
1. Write oxidation number of all the atoms of reactants and products by doing required calculations. (a) stands for known O.N. and (b) for calculated O.N.

\(\mathrm{3H_3AsO_3 + BrO_3^{\ominus} \longrightarrow Br^{\ominus} + 3H_3AsO_4}\)

| species | known O.N. (a) | calculated O.N. (b) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{3H_3AsO_3}\) | H : \(3 \times (+1)\), O : \(3 \times (-2)\) | As : \(+3\) |
| \(\mathrm{BrO_3^{\ominus}}\) | O : \(3 \times (-2)\) | Br : \(+5\) |
| \(\mathrm{Br^{\ominus}}\) | Br : \(-1\) | — |
| \(\mathrm{3H_3AsO_4}\) | H : \(3 \times (+1)\), O : \(4 \times (-2)\) | As : \(+5\) |

2. Identify the species that undergoes change in oxidation number

\(\mathrm{3H_3AsO_3(aq) + BrO_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow Br^{\ominus}(aq) + 3H_3AsO_4(aq)}\)

As : loss of \(\mathrm{2e^{\ominus}}\) (per As atom) ; Br : gain of \(\mathrm{6e^{\ominus}}\)

The oxidation number of As increases from \(+3\) to \(+5\) and that of Br decreases from \(+5\) to \(-1\). Because oxidation number of one species increases and that of other decreases, the reaction is therefore redox reaction.

The oxidation number of As increases by loss of electron. Thus As is a reducing agent and is itself oxidized. On the other hand, the oxidation number of Br decreases. Hence, it is reduced by the gain of electron and act as an oxidizing agent.

**Result :**

1. The reaction is redox reaction.

2. Oxidant/oxidizing agent \(-\) \(\mathrm{BrO_3^{\ominus}}\)

3. Reductant/Reducing agent \(-\) \(\mathrm{H_3AsO_3}\)
_note: p-04 left column, printed p.85. TWO structural facts, both measured: (1) this is the ONE worked example in the chapter that prints NO `Solution :` label — the numbered steps follow the stem directly and the block closes on `Result :`, which is what makes the chapter's Problem count (9) exceed its `Solution :` count (8). (2) The stem is worded in the plural and labels its single reaction `a.`, but no `b.` is printed anywhere in the block. Transcribed as printed. Step 1's oxidation-number assignment is a 2-D arrow diagram in the book; it is rendered here as an equivalent table (same assignments, no information added or lost). The electron-transfer brackets read `Loss of 2e` over the As pair and `Gain of 6e` under the Br pair — the loss figure is PER As ATOM (3 atoms x 2e = 6e, matching the gain); the per-atom/total asymmetry is the book's own labelling and is preserved with the basis stated.

stem:
Using the oxidation number method write the net ionic eqvation for the reaction of potassium permanganate, \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\), with ferrous sulphate, \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\).

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + Fe^{3\oplus}(aq)}\)
solution:
**Step 1 :** The skeletal ionic equation is

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + Fe^{3\oplus}(aq)}\)

**Step 2 :** Assign oxidation number to Mn and Fe, and calculate the increase and decrease in the oxidation number and make them equal. (a) stands for known O.N. and (b) for calculated O.N.

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus} + Fe^{2\oplus} \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus} + Fe^{3\oplus}}\)

| species | known O.N. (a) | calculated O.N. (b) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}}\) | O : \(4 \times (-2)\) | Mn : \(+7\) |
| \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\) | Fe : \(+2\) | — |
| \(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}}\) | Mn : \(+2\) | — |
| \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\) | Fe : \(+3\) | — |

increase in oxidation number :

Fe \((+2) \longrightarrow\) Fe \((+3)\)

increase per atom = 1

decrease in oxidation number :

Mn \((+7) \longrightarrow\) Mn \((+2)\)

decerase per atom = 5

to make the net incearse and decrease equal we must take 5 atoms of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\)

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 5Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 5Fe^{3\oplus}(aq)}\)

**Step 3 :** Balance the 'O' atoms by adding \(\mathrm{4H_2O}\) to the right hand side.

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 5Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 5Fe^{3\oplus}(aq) + 4H_2O}(l)\)

**Step 4 :** The medium is acidic. To make the charges and hydrogen atoms on the two sides equal, add \(\mathrm{8H^{\oplus}}\) on the left hand side.

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 5\ Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) + 8H^{\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 5Fe^{3\oplus}(aq) + 4H_2O}(l)\)

**Step 5 :** Check the two sides for balance of charges and atoms. The net ionic equation obtained in step 4 is the balanced equation.

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 5\ Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) + 8H^{\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 5Fe^{3\oplus}(aq) + 4H_2O}\)
_note: p-05 left column, printed p.86. The stem's `eqvation` and the solution's `decerase` / `net incearse` are the book's own spellings, transcribed as printed. Step 2's arrow diagram rendered as an equivalent table.

stem:
Balance the following reaction by oxidation number mathod.

\(\mathrm{CuO + NH_3 \longrightarrow Cu + N_2 + H_2O}\)
solution:
**Step I :** Write skeletal equation and balance the elements other that O and H.

\(\mathrm{CuO + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow Cu + N_2 + H_2O}\)

**Step II :** Assign oxidation number to Cu and N. Calculate the increase and decrease in the oxidation number and make them equal. (a) stands for known O.N. and (b) for calculated O.N.

\(\mathrm{CuO + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow Cu + N_2 + H_2O}\)

| species | known O.N. (a) | calculated O.N. (b) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{CuO}\) | O : \(-2\) | Cu : \(+2\) |
| \(\mathrm{2NH_3}\) | H : \(3 \times (+1)\) | N : \(-3\) |
| \(\mathrm{Cu}\) | Cu : \(0\) | — |
| \(\mathrm{N_2}\) | N : \(0\) | — |

increase in oxidation number :

\(\mathrm{2NH_3 \longrightarrow N_2}\), N : \(-3 \longrightarrow 0\)

increase per atom = 3

decrease in oxidation number

\(\mathrm{CuO \longrightarrow Cu}\), Cu : \(+2 \longrightarrow 0\)

decrease per atom = 2

to make the net increase and decrease equal we must take 3 atoms of Cu and 2 atoms of N

\(\mathrm{3CuO + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow 3Cu + N_2 + H_2O}\)

**Step III :** Balance 'O' atoms by addition \(\mathrm{2H_2O}\) to the right hand side.

\(\mathrm{3CuO + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow 3Cu + N_2 + 3H_2O}\)

**Step IV :** Charges are already balanced

**Step V :** Check two sides for balanced of atoms and charges. The equation obtain in step IV is balanced.

\(\mathrm{3CuO + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow 3Cu + N_2 + 3H_2O}\)
_note: p-05 right column, printed p.86. `mathod` is the book's own spelling in the stem. Step III's `addition 2H_2O` is consistent — the previous line already carried one H2O, so two more give the printed 3H2O. Step II's arrow diagram rendered as an equivalent table.

stem:
Balance the following unbalanced equation (in acidic medium) by ion electron (half reaction method)

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow MnO_2(s) + ClO_2(aq)}\)
solution:
**Step I :** Write unbalanced equation for the redox reaction. Assign oxidation number to all the atoms in reactants and product then. Divide the equation into two half equations.

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus} + ClO_3^{\ominus} \longrightarrow MnO_2 + ClO_2}\)

| species | known O.N. (a) | calculated O.N. (b) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}}\) | Mn : \(+2\) | — |
| \(\mathrm{ClO_3^{\ominus}}\) | O : \(3 \times (-2)\) | Cl : \(+5\) |
| \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) | O : \(2 \times (-2)\) | Mn : \(+4\) |
| \(\mathrm{ClO_2}\) | O : \(2 \times (-2)\) | Cl : \(+4\) |

Mn : loss of \(\mathrm{2e^{\ominus}}\) ; Cl : gain of \(\mathrm{1e^{\ominus}}\)

Oxidation half reaction

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow MnO_2(s)}\)

Reduction half reaction

\(\mathrm{ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2(aq)}\)

**Step II :** Balance half equations for O atoms by adding \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to the side with less O atoms. Add \(\mathrm{2H_2O}\) to left side of oxidation and one \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to the right side of reduction.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l) \mathrm{\longrightarrow MnO_2(s)}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2(aq) + H_2O}(l)\)

**Step III :** Balance H atoms by adding \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) ions to the side with less H. Hence add \(\mathrm{4H^{\oplus}}\) ions to the right side of oxidation and \(\mathrm{2H^{\oplus}}\) ions to the left side of reduction.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l) \mathrm{\longrightarrow MnO_2 + 4H^{\oplus}(aq)}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) + 2H^{\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2(aq) + H_2O}(l)\)

**Step IV :** Now add 2 electrons to the right side of oxidation and 1 electron to the left side of reduction to balance the charges.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l) \mathrm{\longrightarrow MnO_2(s) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus}}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) + 2H^{\oplus}(aq) + e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_2(aq) + H_2O}(l)\)

**Step V :** Multiply reduction half equation by 2 to equalize number of electrons in two half equations. Then add two half equation.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l) \mathrm{\longrightarrow MnO_2(s) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus}}\) ........ (1)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{2ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow 2ClO_2(aq) + 2H_2O}(l)\) ........ (2)

eq. (1) + eq. (2) gives the net reaction

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 2ClO_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow MnO_2(s) + 2ClO_2(aq)}\)

The equation is balanced in terms of number of atoms and the charges.
_note: Stem + steps I-II in the p-06 left column, steps II(end)-V in the p-06 right column (printed p.87). Step I's arrow diagram rendered as an equivalent table. The book prints `Balance H- atoms` in Step III; transcribed as `H atoms` since the stray hyphen is a typesetting artefact of the superscript, not a species.

stem:
Balance the following unbalanced equation by ion electron (half reaction method)

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq) + ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus}(aq) + O_2(g)}\)
solution:
**Step I :** Write unbalanced equation for the redox reaction and assign oxidation number to all the atoms in reactants and products. (a) stands for known O.N. and (b) for calculated O.N. Divide the equation into two half equations.

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2 + ClO_4^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus} + O_2}\)

| species | known O.N. (a) | calculated O.N. (b) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) | H : \(2 \times (+1)\) | O : \(2 \times (-1)\) |
| \(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}}\) | O : \(4 \times (-2)\) | Cl : \(+7\) |
| \(\mathrm{ClO_2^{\ominus}}\) | O : \(2 \times (-2)\) | Cl : \(+3\) |
| \(\mathrm{O_2}\) | O : \(0\) | — |

O (in \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)) : loss of \(\mathrm{2e^{\ominus}}\) ; Cl : gain of \(\mathrm{4e^{\ominus}}\)

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq) \longrightarrow O_2(g)}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

**Step II :** Balance the half equation for O atoms by adding \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) to the side with less O atoms. Hence add \(\mathrm{2H_2O}\) to the right side of reduction half equation and none to the oxidation half equation

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq) \longrightarrow O_2(g)}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l)\)

**Step III :** Balance H atoms by adding \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) ions to the side with less H. Hence add \(\mathrm{2H^{\oplus}}\) ions to the right side of oxidation half equation and \(\mathrm{4H^{\oplus}}\) ions to the left side of reduction half equation.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq) \longrightarrow O_2(g) + 2H^{\oplus}(aq)}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l)\)

**Step IV :** Add 2 electrons to the right side of oxidation half equation and 4 electrons to the left side of reduction half equation to balance the charges.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2(aq) \longrightarrow O_2(g) + 2H^{\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus}}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 4e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus} + 2H_2O}\)

**Step V :** Multiply oxidation half equation by 2 to equalize the number of electrons and then add two half equations.

Oxidation

\(\mathrm{2H_2O_2(aq) \longrightarrow 2O_2(g) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 4e^{\ominus}}\)

Reduction

\(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 4e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow ClO_2^{\ominus} + 2H_2O}(l)\)

\(\mathrm{2H_2O_2(aq) + ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 4e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow 2O_2(g) + ClO_2^{\ominus}(aq) + 4H^{\oplus}(aq) + 4e^{\ominus} + 2H_2O}(l)\)

\(\mathrm{2H_2O_2(aq) + ClO_4^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow 2O_2(g) + ClO_2^{\ominus}(aq) + 2H_2O}(l)\)

This equation is balanced in terms of atoms and charges.
_note: Stem + `Solution : Step I` open at the foot of the p-06 right column (printed p.87) and the whole worked solution runs on p-07 (printed p.88), left column then right. SPANS THE PAGE BREAK — transcribed whole. Step I's arrow diagram rendered as an equivalent table; the book's `Loss of 2e` bracket spans H2O2 -> O2 (two O atoms, -1 -> 0) and `Gain of 4e` spans ClO4- -> ClO2- (Cl, +7 -> +3).

stem:
By using standard electrode potential table justify that the reaction between the following is spontaneous.

(a) \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{I^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

(b) \(\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\)
solution:
Write oxidation half reaction for one species and reduction half reaction for the other species. Change the sign of \(\mathrm{E^0}\) of oxidation half reaction. Take the sum of two \(\mathrm{E^0}\) values. If the sum is positive the reaction between two species is spontaneous.

**(a) \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{I^{\ominus}(aq)}\)**

| half reaction | | \(\mathrm{E^0}\) |
|---|---|---|
| Reduction : | \(\mathrm{2Fe^{3\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow 2Fe^{2\oplus}}\) | \(+0.77\) V |
| Oxidation : | \(\mathrm{2I^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow I_2(s) + 2e^{\ominus}}\) | \(-0.54\) V |
| | \(\mathrm{2Fe^{3\oplus}(aq) + 2I^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow 2Fe^{2\oplus}(aq) + I_2(s)}\) | Sum = \(+0.23\) V |

The sum of \(\mathrm{E^0}\) values is positive, therefore the reaction is spontaneous.

**(b) \(\mathrm{Ag^{\oplus}(aq)}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu(s)}\)**

| half reaction | | \(\mathrm{E^0}\) |
|---|---|---|
| Reduction : | \(\mathrm{2Ag^{\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow 2Ag(s)}\) | \(+0.80\) V |
| Oxidation : | \(\mathrm{Cu(s) \longrightarrow Cu^{2\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus}}\) | \(-0.34\) V |
| | \(\mathrm{2Ag^{\oplus}(aq) + Cu(s) \longrightarrow 2Ag(s) + Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)}\) | Sum = \(+0.46\) V |

The sum of \(\mathrm{E^0}\) values is positive, therefore reaction is spontaneous.
_note: p-09 full width, printed p.90. The book lays each part out as two half reactions with their E0 values in a right-hand column under a rule; rendered here as a table. ⚠ Part (b) uses E0(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V and E0(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V, and NEITHER couple appears in the chapter's own Table 6.1 on the same page — flagged in the errata as a note, not an error.

Calculate the oxidation number of underlined atoms.

a. \(\mathrm{H_2\underline{S}O_4}\)

b. \(\mathrm{H\underline{N}O_3}\)

c. \(\mathrm{H_3\underline{P}O_3}\)

d. \(\mathrm{K_2\underline{C}_2O_4}\)
